title: Machine Learning Approaches to Biologic Therapy Response in Inflammatory Bowel Disease: A Review Article.
desc: [Sage open pathology] Inflammatory bowel disease (IBD), encompassing Crohn's disease and ulcerative colitis, remains a complex and heterogeneous condition with variable response to biologic therapies. Despite significant advances with anti-TNF agents, integrin inhibitors, and interleukin-12/23 blockers, treatment outcomes are limited by primary nonresponse, secondary loss of efficacy, immunogenicity, and substantial healthcare costs. The advent of artificial intelligence (AI), particularly machine learning (ML) and deep learning (DL) algorithms, offers new opportunities to address these challenges by integrating diverse clinical, laboratory, imaging, histologic, genetic, and microbiome data. Recent studies demonstrate that AI-based models achieve high accuracy in predicting biologic response, remission, and adverse outcomes, outperforming conventional statistical approaches. AI has also shown promise in real-time endoscopic assessment, histologic grading, and forecasting disease progression, enabling earlier intervention and personalized therapy. However, current models are constrained by limited datasets, heterogeneity, lack of large-scale prospective validation, and concerns regarding interpretability, transparency, and patient privacy. Future efforts should prioritize multicenter trials, external validation, and ethical integration into clinical workflows. Collectively, AI-driven prediction of biologic therapy response represents a pivotal step toward precision medicine in IBD, with the potential to optimize therapeutic strategies, reduce ineffective treatment exposure, and improve patient outcomes.

title: Let Samples Sing in Chorus: Mitigating Spurious Correlations via Cross-view Consensus
desc: Deep models often rely on spurious correlations that fail on underrepresented groups. Existing methods either correct human-specified bias attributes or infer unknown biases from the learned representation space. However, annotated attributes may differ from the shortcuts actually used by a model, while a single representation provides incomplete and potentially noisy evidence. Our key insight is that a bias obscured in one feature space may be clearer in another. In this work, we propose CHORD (Cross-view Harmonic Outlier Reversal for Debiasing), a multi-view framework that allows samples to "sing in chorus" across diverse representation spaces to achieve robust cross-view consensus. CHORD aggregates aggregates within-class partitions in each view, which is a proxy for specifying candidate biases, to debias the target representation and classifier without bias supervision. Experiments on seven benchmarks across vision, language, speech, and medical imaging show consistent improvements in worst-group accuracy. Code and checkpoints are available at https://github.com/davelee-uestc/chord_debiasing_public .

title: TabBioMed: A Large-Scale Benchmark for Biomedical Tabular Learning
desc: Recent advances in machine learning have accelerated biomedical prediction, but evaluation on structured biomedical data remains fragmented, especially for datasets with high dimensionality, large sample size, missingness, and class imbalance. We introduce TabBioMed, a large-scale benchmark of 94 curated public biomedical tabular datasets spanning electronic health records, drug discovery, genomics, transcriptomics, proteomics, metabolomics, single-cell omics, and systems biology. TabBioMed unifies these datasets through a standardized, dataset-aware preprocessing and evaluation framework, enabling reproducible comparison across classification, regression, and multi-target tasks. We benchmark 23 models across classical baselines, gradient-boosted trees, neural tabular architectures, and tabular foundation models. Foundation models deliver the strongest family-level predictive performance. However, their gains are regime-dependent: tree-based models and tuned multilayer perceptrons remain highly competitive, often dominating under inference-time or training-cost constraints. Overall, TabBioMed shows that biomedical tabular learning is strongly context-dependent, with optimal model choice depending on data regime, task type, and computational budget. We release TabBioMed with curated datasets and splits, preprocessing code, baselines, and results, providing a reproducible benchmark for practical model selection and future methods development in biomedical machine learning, available at https://github.com/AI-sandbox/TabBioMed.

title: Learning spatial cellular state through 3D reconstruction of the cell
desc: Subcellular-resolution spatial transcriptomics localizes individual RNA transcripts within cells with high-precision. Existing methods for identifying spatially organized cell populations rely on cellular niches defined by neighboring cells, leaving open whether such populations can be identified from individual-cell representations alone. Moreover, representations that jointly capture transcript identity and three-dimensional (3D) spatial organization have not been systematically learned or biologically evaluated. Here we present a representation learning framework that models each cell as a gene-annotated point cloud of transcripts and trains a rotation-equivariant neural network to reconstruct 3D cell shape, yielding spatially informed transcript embeddings. We further aggregate these embeddings into a cell-state representation that summarizes transcript-level spatial patterns. Our framework outperforms existing point-cloud-based 3D reconstruction methods on cell-shape reconstruction. In MERFISH human uterine cancer, combining the learned embeddings with gene expression improved prediction of CD45RO protein intensity over both gene expression alone and niche-based embeddings. Applied to MERFISH human liver cancer and Xenium human lung datasets, our framework identified distinct spatial patterns between cell populations, including spatially organized subpopulations marked by disease-associated gene expression and patterns associated with pathological tissue structures. Together, these results show that learning transcript representations through 3D cell reconstruction provides a novel approach to capture cell-state heterogeneity and biologically relevant spatial organization in subcellular spatial transcriptomics.

title: Physician AI disclosure, condition severity, and public trust in digital medicine
desc: Public trust is central to the implementation of artificial intelligence (AI) in digital medicine, yet little is known about how patients respond to different forms of physician AI disclosure across clinical risk contexts. In a 5 × 2 factorial experiment in mainland China, 1574 adults were randomly assigned to physician profiles varying by AI use type and condition severity. Administrative AI was rated more favorably than diagnostic and therapeutic AI across physician perception and care-seeking intention outcomes. High-severity conditions amplified negative responses to therapeutic AI, whereas explicit non-AI disclosure was associated with greater appointment willingness under high severity. Exploratory mediation analyses suggested that competence, trust, and empathy accounted for different disclosure-related response patterns. Main effects were directionally consistent in a supplementary offline community sample from Macao ( n = 128). These findings suggest that AI disclosure in digital medicine should distinguish administrative from clinical uses and be calibrated to clinical severity, while highlighting the need for preregistered replication using behavioral outcomes.

title: Artificial Intelligence in the Advancement of Mechanical Circulatory Support and Cardiac Care: A Systematic Review of Its Role and Potential.
desc: [Artificial organs] In recent years, there has been a notable surge in the ability of machines to perform complex and intelligent human-centered tasks, particularly within the domain of cardiovascular health. Rapid advancements in artificial intelligence (AI) and machine learning (ML) algorithms reflect the considerable potential for such analyses to meaningfully extend into translational device development and clinical usage of medical devices, especially mechanical circulatory support (MCS) therapies. Here, we investigate and report the applications, limitations, and strategies in which AI is currently being employed in MCS and the potential opportunities of AI approaches to advance the field of MCS. To effectively assess the scope and impact of AI in MCS, we conducted a systematic literature review. A comprehensive search of 4 recognized research databases (PubMed, Google Scholar, Ovid MEDLINE, and ProQuest) was performed using this Boolean string: "(Artificial Intelligence) AND (AI) AND (Mechanical Circulatory Support) AND (MCS) NOT (Heart Transplant) NOT (Cardiogenic Shock) NOT (Critical Care)." This strategy was designed to identify the application of AI in MCS only. Database search results were then screened by titles and abstracts, followed by full-text eligibility assessment and duplicate removal. Following these screening and eligibility steps, 30 of the 328 identified articles remained for inclusion. Most relevant publications covered two main subjects: the prediction and management of postoperative outcomes, and the development of personalized device-patient matching and timing. Across the reviewed studies, AI/ML models demonstrated promising performance in study-specific predictions of complications, recovery-related outcomes, and survival and were investigated as tools to support clinical decision-making. Barriers to broad implementation of AI include the necessity for sizable, high-quality datasets to achieve algorithm training benchmarks, the lack of organized and complete databases, such as INTERMACS, and limited computational resources. Emerging frontiers of MCS recognize the potential for AI and ML techniques to refine image recognition capabilities, diagnostic assessment, device placement, and post-implantation monitoring approaches in the future. AI-driven approaches demonstrate a promising convergence of computational power and clinical expertise, with the potential to support more personalized, efficient, and informed management of MCS patients. title: Auditable Clinical Support with Decision Agents
desc: Clinicians reviewing a diagnostic work-up will ask what was considered at each step and why the assessment changed. Agents powered by free text can reach physician-level diagnostic accuracy, but their written reasoning does not always reflect the factors that went into the decision. Here, we present Decision2Care, a decision agent that works up the acutely ill patient without producing any text. A decision model assigns a probability to each permitted EHR action, and fixed rules carry out the most probable one. We evaluated Decision2Care on the records of 546 emergency admissions across 12 diseases. Decision2Care reached a diagnostic accuracy of 86.5%, compared with 86.1% for the MIRA-v2 agent, and required a median of 2.2 s per work-up, compared with 92-100 s. Each work-up tracked which options Decision2Care was considering at each step. In 10 of the 12 diseases, the differential diagnosis changed most at the test on which the guideline bases the diagnosis. Where Decision2Care was most confident after a single work-up, all but four of its diagnoses were correct (98.5%). We traced each of these four errors back to a single imaging report. Three of them were corrected when that report was removed. The same kind of decision was used to select the treatments, and Decision2Care's drug orders were judged guideline-adherent more often than MIRA-v2's. In emergency patients, its prediction of death was comparable to that of three intensivists on the same cases. In five of the eight intensive care cohorts, it exceeded the best of the three 24-h severity scores within 2-6 h of records. Our results show that decision agents can carry out clinical work-ups while recording the options, probabilities, and execution rules behind each action for audit.

title: Accurate and interpretable protein complex stoichiometry prediction through agentic AI with StoiAgent
desc: Accurate protein complex structure modeling requires knowledge of complex stoichiometry, yet the copy numbers of individual subunits are often unknown. Consequently, predicting protein complex stoichiometry has emerged as a major challenge in recent years. Here, we present StoiAgent, a large language model (LLM)-powered AI agent that automates the retrieval and integration of sequence, structural, and literature evidence to predict stoichiometry while preserving interpretable reasoning traces (chain of thoughts) of its evidence assessment and ranking decision. An open-weight LLM model, Qwen3.6-27B, is used by StoiAgent as the LLM backbone to combine sequences, structural templates, AlphaFold3 structure predictions, and literature evidence, and perform stoichiometry candidate generation and ranking. On 56 CASP17 protein complex targets, it achieves top-1 accuracy of 75.0%, which represents a 23.2 percentage-point improvement over PreStoi with AlphaFold3 ranking (51.8%) and matches the top-1 accuracy of StoPred. Moreover, StoiAgent has a higher top-3 and top-5 accuracy than StoPred (85.7% versus 80.4% and 87.5% versus 85.7%, respectively). Furthermore, it outperforms general-purpose frontier LLMs, including ChatGPT and Gemini, in stoichiometry prediction. Case studies further illustrate how StoiAgent evaluates competing assembly hypotheses by integrating complementary evidence, with recorded reasoning traces documenting its decision-making process. Overall, StoiAgent demonstrates the potential of LLM-powered AI agents to improve protein complex stoichiometry prediction through the automated integration of diverse sources of evidence while providing interpretable explanations to guide downstream structure modeling.

title: Imaging-based biological age gap and risk of mortality and incident diseases: a systematic review and meta-analysis
desc: Artificial intelligence-derived imaging ageing clocks enable estimation of biological ageing from medical images. Yet meta-analytic quantification of the associations between imaging age gaps and both mortality and incident age-related diseases across multiple organs remains lacking. This study synthesised 40 eligible reports, of which 21 contributed to the meta-analysis. Meta-analyses showed that each 5-year increase in imaging age gap was associated with a higher hazard of all-cause mortality (HR 1.31, 95% CI 1.19–1.44), although heterogeneity was substantial ( I ² = 96.3%), with organ type and sample size contributing to heterogeneity. For cancer-specific mortality, the pooled HR was 1.06 (95% CI 0.96–1.18). Higher imaging age gaps were associated with incident dementia, stroke, heart failure, diabetes and hypertension, but not Parkinson’s disease. Imaging age gaps may support non-invasive risk stratification and long-term health management, but clinical translation requires standardisation, diverse external validation, interpretability, and evidence of clinical utility and equity.

title: AI Predictive Models for Discharge Disposition in Patients Following Primary Total Knee Arthroplasty: Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis.
source: PubMed · Journal of medical Internet research
desc: [Journal of medical Internet research] Although a growing number of AI-based predictive models for discharge disposition in patients following primary total knee arthroplasty (TKA) have been constructed, their performance, quality, and applicability remain unclear. This study aimed to evaluate the performance, quality, and applicability of published AI-based predictive models for discharge disposition in patients following primary TKA. PubMed, Web of Science, Embase, the Cochrane Library, Scopus, China National Knowledge Infrastructure, Wanfang Database, China Science and Technology Journal Database, and SinoMed Database were searched from inception to May 26, 2025. We included original studies that developed AI-based predictive models for discharge disposition in adult patients (age ≥18 years) undergoing primary TKA. Studies involving simultaneous bilateral or revision TKA or those that did not develop a predictive model were excluded. Risk of bias and reporting quality were assessed using the PROBAST+AI (Prediction Model Risk of Bias Assessment Tool+AI) and TRIPOD+AI (Transparent Reporting of a Multivariable Prediction Model for Individual Prognosis or Diagnosis+AI), respectively. Pooled area under the curve values and 95% CIs were estimated using a DerSimonian-Laird random-effects model with the Hartung-Knapp-Sidik-Jonkman adjustment. A total of 5 retrospective studies from the United States involving 4 ML-based models and 1 DL-based model were included, with sample sizes ranging from 175,042 to 434,550 patients. Age and sex were the most frequently used predictors. All included studies were rated as having a high risk of bias according to the PROBAST+AI checklist. title: AI-Assisted vs. Traditional Simulation for Safe Surgery Checklist Knowledge and Skills
desc: [Newly registered clinical trial, no results yet; sponsor: Lokman Hekim University; conditions: Nursing Education; type: INTERVENTIONAL; phase: NA; enrollment: 60; status: NOT_YET_RECRUITING] More than 300 million surgical procedures are performed worldwide each year. However, surgical errors remain among the most common medical errors causing preventable patient harm. Although various health policies have been implemented globally and nationally, adverse events continue to occur due to factors such as high patient volumes and insufficient staffing. One of the most important initiatives developed to prevent surgery-related adverse events is the World Health Organization's "Safe Surgery Saves Lives" project. Within this initiative, the Surgical Safety Checklist was developed and has contributed to significant reductions in adverse events. The World Health Organization has encouraged countries to adapt the checklist to their healthcare systems. In Türkiye, it was revised by adding an additional section based on the principle that "Safe surgery starts in the clinic." Current patient safety policies and initiatives largely focus on healthcare professionals. However, developing a culture of surgical safety should begin during undergraduate education. After graduation, students may adopt existing institutional practices regarding patient and surgical safety. Therefore, developing nursing students' knowledge, skills, and professional judgment regarding safe surgery before graduation is essential. This randomized controlled experimental study aims to compare the effectiveness of an artificial intelligence-assisted virtual simulation game and traditional simulation in improving nursing students' knowledge and skills regarding the Surgical Safety Checklist. The effects of these interventions on students' problem-solving skills and patient safety competencies will also be examined. Students, research fellows, and the statistician will be blinded. Data will be collected using the Surgical Safety Checklist Knowledge Test, Surgical Safety Checklist Skills Assessment Checklist, Problem Solving Inventory, and a scale assessing nursing students' patient safety competencies. title: Auditing black-box clinical prediction models with a large language model through queries alone: a blinded test with planted flaws
desc: Large language models (LLMs) are used to explain clinical prediction models, on the promise that they can say what a model computes, find its faults and even reveal new knowledge in it. We tested the three promises where the answers could be checked. From the International Stroke Trial we trained four kinds of model (logistic regression, explainable boosting machine, gradient-boosted trees, neural network) for two outcomes on patients randomised earlier, planted one flaw in each of 24 copies (an under-predicted subgroup, a reversed risk factor or an implausible step) and mixed them with the 8 clean models. GPT-6 Astra audited each model three times, blind, through a tool that only returned the model's predictions; the judging rules were committed before any run and applied by program. Its surrogate models, with a median of 128 terms, reproduced the audited models' log-odds with a mean $R^2$ of 0.976 (0.959 for an additive surrogate of 42 terms fitted by an analyst). It found the planted flaw in 69 of 72 runs (96%; 95% CI 80% to 99%); a script written for the purpose found all 24. It also reported many more problems: 60% of 1,089 checkable reports failed the pre-specified check against the model's average behaviour; post hoc, most of these were real but small steps, and 15% of the checkable reports were not found in the model. Of 601 unexpected relationships it read out of the clean models, 11% held in patients randomised later (random pairs 6%; a regression scan's shorter list of its strongest candidates, 28%); after a check on the training data, 33% against 30%. With query access alone, an LLM can describe a black-box model faithfully and find nearly every planted flaw, as a purpose-written script also did; its reports of problems must be checked on the model and its discoveries on data.

title: BI-SCUDO Regression - A novel algorithm to infer clinical variables from omics datasets
desc: Regression analysis of high-throughput omics data is often made difficult by noise, batch effects, and the loss of information resulting from the discretization of continuous variables. Existing machine learning algorithms often struggle to extract stable biological signals under these heterogeneous conditions. We introduce BI-SCUDO Regression, a rank-based regression framework designed for omics data analysis. By leveraging within-sample rankings and network-based predictions, BI-SCUDO Regression bypasses the need for complex normalization and provides robust, interpretable results. In synthetic benchmarks, BI-SCUDO Regression demonstrated strong resilience to noise, maintaining predictive and feature-selection stability under conditions in which standard models exhibited performance degradation. When applied to cohorts from TCGA datasets, BI-SCUDO Regression consistently outperformed LASSO, Random Forest Regression, and XGBoost in predicting survival, with an average increase in Ratio of Performance to Deviation ranging from 43% to 86%, depending on the comparator. Furthermore, the algorithm consistently identified parsimonious, statistically significant, and biologically relevant biomarkers, with enrichment for cancer-related terms across all stage stratifications. Although BI-SCUDO Regression incurs higher training times due to its genetic optimization strategy, it offers a robust and interpretable approach to outcome prediction and biomarker discovery, with potential applications in precision medicine, where noisy data compromise the performance of conventional regression methods.

title: Network meta-analysis of digital interventions for fibromyalgia
desc: This systematic review and network meta-analysis evaluated digital interventions for function, pain, and depression in adults with fibromyalgia. PubMed, Embase, the Cochrane Library, Web of Science, and Scopus were searched up to 1 February 2026. Risk of bias and evidence certainty were assessed using RoB 2.0 and Confidence in Network Meta-Analysis (CINeMA). Twenty-three randomized controlled trials involving 1540 participants were included. Random-effects network meta-analysis showed that digital psychological-behavioral interventions (DPI) and tele-rehabilitation guidance (TRG) significantly reduced pain versus waitlist (WL) or treatment-as-usual (TAU) controls (DPI: SMD: −1.25, 95% CI: −2.01 to −0.48, moderate certainty of evidence; TRG: SMD: −1.15, 95% CI: −1.86 to −0.43, low certainty of evidence). No significant overall effects were observed for fibromyalgia impact or depression. Exploratory subgroup analyses suggested different patterns across age and intervention-duration strata, but effect modification was not formally tested. Heterogeneity and imprecision limit interpretation. Larger standardized trials are needed to clarify treatment modifiers and inform personalized care.

title: AI-guided CRISPR gene editing for cardiovascular disease: Current progress, transitional challenges, and future directions.
source: PubMed · American heart journal plus : cardiology research and practice
desc: [American heart journal plus : cardiology research and practice] Cardiovascular disease (CVD) remains a leading cause of global morbidity and mortality despite major advances in pharmacological therapy, interventional cardiology, and lifestyle-based prevention. Although many current treatments reduce disease burden and improve outcomes, they often fail to address the underlying molecular and genetic mechanisms driving disease progression dot CRISPR hyphen-based gene- editing systems (Clustered Regularly Interspaced Short Palindromic Repeats) have introduced the possibility of directly correcting, silencing, or modulating pathogenic genetic determinants involved in cardiovascular pathology. When integrated with artificial intelligence (AI)-enabled design, prediction, and optimization tools, an AI-guided CRISPR framework may assist in prioritizing editing strategies, predicting editing outcomes, and informing delivery design, although cardiovascular-specific validation of these applications remains limited. This narrative review examines the potential role of AI-guided CRISPR technologies in cardiovascular disease. It first outlines the major pathophysiologic mechanisms underlying CVD, then reviews molecular and genetic targets that may be amenable to editing. Current CRISPR applications in cardiometabolic and cardiovascular disorders are discussed, followed by an evaluation of how AI may support guide RNA design, off-target prediction, vector engineering, and therapeutic prioritization. Finally, major translational barriers are examined, including tissue-specific delivery, editing in non-dividing cells, long-term genomic safety, disease complexity, and regulatory implementation. Although early preclinical findings are encouraging, most cardiovascular applications remain in the experimental or early translational stage, and direct evidence for integrated AI-guided CRISPR applications in cardiovascular disease remains limited and largely preclinical. Progress in this field will depend on advances in delivery science, genome engineering, computational modelling, and long-term safety validation. AI-guided CRISPR should therefore be regarded as a developing precision medicine strategy with substantial future potential rather than an immediately deployable clinical solution.

title: Endoscopic Ultrasound Predictors of Malignancy in IPMNs: Toward Personalized, Data-driven Risk Stratification
desc: [Newly registered clinical trial, no results yet; sponsor: IRCCS San Raffaele; conditions: Intraductal Papillary Mucinous Neoplasms, Pancreatic Cystic Neoplasms, IPMN, Pancreatic Neoplasms, Pancreatic Cancer; type: OBSERVATIONAL; enrollment: 198; status: COMPLETED] Intraductal papillary mucinous neoplasms (IPMNs) are among the most clinically relevant pancreatic cystic lesions because of their potential for malignant transformation into high-grade dysplasia or invasive carcinoma. Accurate preoperative risk stratification is essential to identify patients who may benefit from surgical resection while avoiding unnecessary surgery in those with low-grade disease. Endoscopic ultrasound (EUS) plays a central role in the evaluation of IPMNs because it allows detailed assessment of ductal and cystic features associated with malignancy, including mural nodules, main pancreatic duct abnormalities, wall thickening, contrast enhancement, and elastography patterns. However, the combined predictive value of these features has not been fully standardized. The IMAGE study is a single-center retrospective study designed to develop and validate a machine learning-based model integrating comprehensive EUS features to predict the presence of high-grade dysplasia or invasive carcinoma in patients with surgically resected IPMNs. The study includes adult patients who underwent preoperative EUS at a tertiary referral center and had a final histological diagnosis of IPMN after surgery. The primary objective is to assess the diagnostic performance of the IMAGE model for predicting high-grade dysplasia or invasive carcinoma. Secondary objectives include evaluation of the diagnostic contribution of individual EUS feature domains and assessment of agreement between preoperative EUS classification and final histological diagnosis.

title: Prognosis Without Prediction: The Intrinsic Geometry of Survival
desc: Modeling systemic failure in high-dimensional environments is fundamentally limited by supervised algorithms that attempt to predict sparse, noisy or censored endpoints. To break this reliance on explicit outcome regression, we engineered the Self-Organizing Survival Manifolds (SOSM) framework, a deep learning architecture that decouples unsupervised representation learning from survival labels and treats time-to-event progression as an emergent geometric property. The system projects heterogeneous multi-omics arrays into a unified latent space governed by a pseudotime-weighted, curvature-minimizing graph Laplacian, organizing patient trajectories along low-dissipation geodesic flows. To validate the framework, we applied this architecture to a 184-patient clear cell renal cell carcinoma multi-omics cohort. Across a deterministic 5-fold cross-validation pipeline, SOSM achieved a mean Concordance Index of $0.768 \pm 0.068$, while out-of-fold risk stratification yielded significant survival divergence (log-rank $p < 0.001$) accompanied by a 14.7% increase in local manifold dissipation among high-risk patients. Furthermore, interrogating the network's encoder weights confirmed that the model autonomously recovered canonical metabolic and microenvironmental drivers of disease progression without supervised feature selection. By demonstrating that systemic failure can be mapped as a geometric phase transition, SOSM establishes a generalizable computational engine for prognostic modeling across biological, industrial and financial complex systems.

title: GenVinci reconstructs 3D molecular tissue scenes from histology to map senescence across aging and disease
desc: Spatial omics has generated measurements at unprecedented scale, yet computational approaches remain largely confined to individual modalities and 2D representations. Here we assemble ImageOmicsNet-300M, a corpus of 300 million single-cell and spatial transcriptomic profiles, including 24.9 million H&E-predicted virtual spatial transcriptomics profiles, and 4,623 H&E sections. Of these H&E sections, we generated 1,782 from aging mouse organs and serially sectioned human skin spanning five decades, with matched spatial transcriptomics and snRNA-seq. Building on this resource, we develop GenVinci, a multimodal tissue foundation model that reconstructs 3D tissue scenes from routine 2D histology. GenVinci predicts spatial gene expression from H&E with zero-shot generalization and maps senescence-associated states across 85.8 million cells, revealing cell-type-specific patterns and disease-associated remodeling. Integration with human genetics implicates suprabasal keratinocytes in atopic dermatitis and keratinocyte carcinomas, linked to higher and lower p16 and p21 expression, respectively. These findings establish GenVinci as a framework mapping senescence in 3D across scales.

title: Artificial intelligence support for the prediction and management of drug-drug interactions.
source: PubMed · Expert opinion on drug metabolism & toxicology
desc: [Expert opinion on drug metabolism & toxicology] Drug-drug interactions (DDIs) are a preventable cause of adverse drug events (ADEs), yet conventional interaction-checking tools are hampered by incomplete knowledge, poor concordance, and clinically unusable alert burdens. Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly utilized to strengthen multiple stages of the DDI pathway. This narrative review synthesizes literature identified through searches conducted between 15 July and 20 October 2026. It examines how machine learning (ML) predicts novel drug interactions from molecular structure and knowledge graphs; how natural language processing (NLP) and large language models (LLMs) identify and extract interactions from the literature, drug labels, and pharmacovigilance data; and how AI can make clinical decision support context-aware and support medication review. It also integrates mechanistic physiologically based pharmacokinetic (PBPK) modeling and individualized patient-level risk prediction. Prediction models achieve impressive benchmark accuracy but frequently underperform in realistic, cold-start settings; LLMs detect interactions with high sensitivity but show poor severity calibration and persistent hallucination. The near-term value of AI lies less in autonomous prediction than in curating knowledge, personalizing alerts, and augmenting clinician judgment. Rigorous external validation, interpretability, and regulatory clarity are prerequisites for clinical adoption.

title: ProbMedTOD: A Bayesian Network Guided Task-Oriented Dialogue System for Patient History Taking
desc: Patient history taking is a strategic, multi-turn process that refines diagnostic hypotheses through iterative questioning, mirroring clinical reasoning where each inquiry updates beliefs over candidate diagnoses. Deploying AI in this setting is constrained by privacy, cost, and latency, making Small Language Models (SLMs) a more desirable backbone compared to larger LLMs. However, SLMs capture only the fast, intuitive "System 1" side of this process and lack explicit mechanisms for the deliberative "System 2" reasoning needed to maintain and update diagnostic uncertainty over time. Bayesian Networks (BayesNets) offer a natural complement, providing an interpretable framework for auditable probabilistic belief tracking. Yet, clinical BayesNets are difficult to construct due to their reliance on expert curated structure, dependencies, and parameters. We introduce ProbMedTOD, which automatically synthesizes a clinical BayesNet from a small number of clinical notes in three stages: ontology building, structure prediction, and parameter estimation. ProbMedTOD then integrates the resulting BayesNet with SLMs, enabling probabilistic reasoning in multi-turn dialogues. A BayesNet Agent maintains real-time posterior distributions over diagnoses, while a Policy Agent picks diagnostically informative questions. Experiments on DDXPlus and MIMIC-IV Notes show that ProbMedTOD outperforms LLM-only and retrieval-based baselines, with especially strong gains for smaller models.

title: BiomedCAT: Biomedical Context Analysis Tool for Supporting Mechanistic Hypothesis Generation via User-defined Contextual Subgraph Extraction
desc: Researchers formulate mechanistic hypotheses in slides and figures long before they write them as text, yet knowledge-graph (KG) tools expect a query in the vocabulary of the graph. We present BiomedCAT, an open-source workflow that turns biomedical slides into a subgraph of the RTX-KG2c knowledge graph shaped by the user's research profile, on a laptop and without sending the documents out. A small vision-language model describes each slide; a 4-billion-parameter agent types the terms into the classes of the Biolink model; an existence gate removes invented entities; identifiers are retrieved from Translator services or from a local table and selected, never generated, by a judge model; and a profile-weighted two-hop expansion builds the context graph. On a synthetic Biolink typing benchmark whose labels were audited by an expert, the local agent reaches 0.71 accuracy on 517 non-ambiguous mentions, 4 points below Claude Opus 5 (0.75), level with DeepSeek-V4-Flash (0.69) and above open-weight models of 24 and 31 billion parameters; the audit also showed that 55% of the generated labels were wrong or ambiguous. On expert-annotated slide decks, the reading stage recovers 81 to 94% of the explicit terms of the English deck, less on French decks, and linking assigns the expert identifier to 65% of the found terms online and 26% in the fully local mode. A one-slide run takes 33 to 42 minutes, with peaks of 9.8~GB of system RAM above idle and 5.3~GB of GPU memory. In a facioscapulohumeral muscular dystrophy (FSHD) case, three slides that each draw one pathway from DUX4 at a different biological scale give graphs that overlap by 7 to 15% of their nodes, each recovering its own pathway's expected nodes, and expose sourced paths from DUX4, such as a DUX4--HMGB1 interaction from IntAct. Of 21 compounds tested in FSHD, seven, including every agent that targets DUX4, are absent from RTX-KG2c, which bounds what a graph-based approach can propose. BiomedCAT lets a researcher set a working hypothesis against curated knowledge, with every edge traceable to its source.

title: ChatGPT health and AI for healthcare: From commercial personal assistant to public health infrastructure.
desc: [Digital health] The launch of OpenAI's ChatGPT Health for individuals and ChatGPT for Healthcare for institutions marks a major expansion of large language models into health and healthcare delivery. While these products promise efficiency gains and improved access to information, they also raise significant concerns for privacy, patient safety, and the governance of digital health infrastructures. This paper provides an evaluation of OpenAI's health-focused products by examining their systemic implications and outlining public-interest governance models that could better align generative artificial intelligence (AI) with health system goals. Using a document-based analysis of publicly available vendor communications, technical documentation, and policy pages-interpreted through sociotechnical frameworks in health informatics-we evaluate product architectures, data flows, validation claims, and governance mechanisms. Vendor materials indicate that both products may facilitate large-scale aggregation of sensitive health and behavioral data, enabling longitudinal health profiles that raise unresolved questions about data retention, secondary use, reidentification, and cross-border transfers. Despite public claims of safety and high benchmark performance, available validation appears concentrated on narrow tasks and proprietary internal assessments, which cannot substitute for appropriate clinical governance or comprehensive regulatory evaluation. These developments may also deepen dependence on a single global vendor, creating structural risks for digital sovereignty and health equity, particularly in jurisdictions with weaker data protections. Ultimately, generative AI in health should not be framed primarily as a multi-purpose consumer application operated by a monolithic platform, but as a specialized tool embedded within publicly governed digital health infrastructures.

title: Reference-Guided Data Curation for 3D Medical Vision-Language Pretraining
desc: Training 3D vision-language models (VLMs) on large medical imaging datasets collected across institutions is constrained by data quality. Vast, uncurated pools of image-report pairs are characterized by redundancy, class imbalance, and cross-institutional heterogeneity. We address this challenge of data curation for improving 3D VLM pretraining by proposing an offline, training-free, reference-guided data curation recipe. Our approach leverages a small, high-quality reference set to independently extract quality signals for each modality of a large, uncurated pool and merges them through a rank-aggregation step into a single ranking that guides sample selection. We validate this method on datasets comprising 35k 3D abdominal CT volume-report pairs from two institutions and 58k 2D chest X-ray image-report pairs. On 3D CT, using our reference-guided data curation strategy, our curated model matches the zero-shot disease classification performance of a state-of-the-art baseline (Merlin) while using $3.3\times$ less training data and a reference set of 5k samples. On 2D chest X-rays, our method yields a curated model that matches or exceeds the zero-shot disease classification performance of a model trained on the full pool while using up to $10\times$ less training data and a reference set of only 74 samples. Ablations show that the selection is stable under resampling of the reference, that smaller reference sets still outperform random sampling, and that label rebalancing does not improve performance. To support reproducibility, we release our code.

title: scUNVEIL: Learning scRNA-seq Cell Embeddings Through Measurement Enrichment
desc: Large-scale pretraining can improve scRNA-seq representations through measurement enrichment: estimating what the same measurement would reveal at greater UMI depth under the same measurement process. We introduce scUNVEIL, a self-supervised model trained through next-UMI prediction. We show that the Bayes-optimal next-UMI predictor is the posterior mean of the transcriptome composition that arbitrarily deep sequencing would reveal. Because UMI identities are exchangeable conditional on transcriptome composition, scUNVEIL operates directly on count vectors using a residual multilayer perceptron, without attention over gene tokens. The measurement-enriched transcriptome composition is predicted from a single low-dimensional hidden state, which therefore serves naturally as the cell embedding. The same model provides both reusable cell representations and measurement-enriched gene-expression estimates. scUNVEIL was pretrained without labels or auxiliary metadata on approximately 92 million human cells spanning diverse tissues. Under linear evaluation on fine-grained cell-type annotation, its zero-shot representations achieved the best performance among the evaluated methods, while providing over 1000-fold faster inference than the strongest evaluated transformer-based foundation model and matching that model's predictive performance using 88% fewer input UMIs per cell. Further evaluations show that these representations improve prediction of tumor reactivity, mitochondrial membrane potential, cell morphology, and lineage-associated treatment outcomes.

title: Reclaiming the Narrative: Why Humanism and Narratology Must Counter the Rise of Algorithmic Medicine.
source: PubMed · Journal of general internal medicine
desc: [Journal of general internal medicine] As artificial intelligence (AI) promises diagnostic precision approaching human expertise, medicine faces a profound paradox: expanding technological capabilities risk eroding the human encounter between caregiver and patient. The Age of Reason in medicine has privileged quantifiable, systematized knowledge validated through randomized controlled trials, yet this epistemological dominance threatens to hollow out medicine's humanistic core. While algorithms excel at pattern recognition and prediction, they cannot grapple with ambiguity, uncertainty, or the irreducible complexity of human suffering. AI deployment risks creating an "AI trust gap" and automation bias among clinicians. Narrative medicine offers an essential counterweight, defining illness as a meaningful disruption of a person's life story rather than merely a departure from physiological norms. Empirical evidence demonstrates that narrative medicine training improves empathy, communication skills, and clinical outcomes. This perspective argues for mandatory, longitudinal narrative medicine curricula and institutional reforms that recognize humanistic practice as a core professional competency, ensuring AI serves rather than obscures medicine's irreducible humanity.

Digital health literacy will be assessed using the eHealth Literacy Scale (eHEALS), while surgical fear will be evaluated using the Surgical Fear Questionnaire (SFQ). The study will examine the relationships between digital health literacy, AI use, and surgical fear, including concerns about short-term and long-term consequences of surgery. title: Sex Differences in the Detection of Parkinson's Disease from Speech
desc: Parkinson's disease (PD) is the second most common neurodegenerative disease in the world, and 70\% to 75\% of PD patients suffer from speech disorders at some stage. Since PD affects men more frequently than women, previous publications tend to rely on unbalanced datasets that potentially introduce sex biases into trained models. This study investigates sex differences in PD detection from speech using deep learning and traditional machine learning approaches. We evaluated speech-based PD detection using embeddings from three pre-trained speech models, combined with handcrafted acoustic features and different classifiers. Sex-specific experiments were conducted on balanced subsets of four sustained phonation datasets, controlling for sex, disease status, and, where possible, age. All recordings were obtained during a sustained phonation task. Results show that female speakers were more accurately classified than male speakers in the larger dataset. Sex-specific results show that when the models are trained on one sex, they fail to generalize to the other one. Our results highlight the importance of including sex as a variable in the development of PD detection systems.

title: DRAFT: graph-recurrent learning of dynamic gene regulatory networks along single-cell multi-omics trajectories
desc: Single-cell multi-omics data offer an opportunity to resolve how gene regulatory networks (GRNs) are rewired during cell-fate transitions, but most existing methods infer static snapshots, ignore temporal dependencies or assume linear regulation. Here we present DRAFT, a deep learning framework that combines graph attention with recurrent temporal memory to infer dynamic GRNs from time-resolved single-cell multi-omics data. On simulated data, DRAFT outperforms existing methods in accuracy and temporal smoothness. In mouse cellular reprogramming and Drosophila adult spermatogenesis, it recovers interactions supported by independent ChIP-seq, perturbation and Hi-C data, together with known stage-specific regulators. By inferring regulatory activity from dynamic network structure rather than expression alone, DRAFT identifies regulators whose activity precedes their transcriptional peak, including the candidate early germline regulator Mondo. Germline-specific Mondo knockdown alters germline stem cell number and expression of the predicted targets kuz and mamo. DRAFT also enables nonlinear alignment of co-developing lineages and reveals stage-specific cell-cell communication.

title: The Formal-Functional Gap: How Artificial Intelligence Reshapes Medical Professional Identity.
source: PubMed · Advances in medical education and practice
desc: [Advances in medical education and practice] Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly integrated into clinical practice and medical education, yet research on AI and medical professional identity has largely evolved in parallel. To examine how AI is transforming fundamental components of medical professional identity and propose a framework for understanding its implications for professional identity formation in medical education. This narrative review synthesizes conceptual, empirical, and theoretical literature on AI, professional identity formation, and clinical practice through iterative literature searching and citation tracking. Peer-reviewed studies, regulatory data, and national survey reports were considered. AI affects professional identity unevenly. Diagnostic, predictive, generative, and emerging autonomous systems most directly influence expertise, clinical reasoning, and professional autonomy, shifting physicians from exclusive holders of specialized knowledge toward validators of increasingly accessible but variably trusted information. Evidence of automation bias and reduced diagnostic performance highlights this transition. We conceptualize the divergence between the formal locus of clinical responsibility, which remains with physicians, and the functional locus of influence decisions, shared with AI, as the formal-functional gap (FFG). Its magnitude varies by AI configuration, identity component, and career stage, potentially placing trainees at risk of never-skilling and experienced physicians at risk of deskilling. Ethical responsibility, humanistic care, lifelong learning, and professional authority are affected more indirectly. AI-mediated professional identity change reflects a dynamic interaction between physicians' developmental trajectories and evolving AI capabilities. Medical education should prioritize sustained expertise, clinical reasoning, professional autonomy, AI-interpretive judgment, and human oversight. The FFG remains a conceptual framework whose relationships require empirical validation.

title: Robotic Surgery in Adult Spine Deformity
desc: [Newly registered clinical trial, no results yet; sponsor: RadiologieSPZ; conditions: Adult Spine Deformity (ASD); type: OBSERVATIONAL; enrollment: 40; status: RECRUITING] Adult spinal deformity (ASD) significantly impacts quality of life through chronic low back pain and/or spinal imbalance, impairing the ability to walk independently in patients both with and without spinal cord injury (SCI). In particular, the importance of sagittal balance of the spine and its correlation with outcome in the bipedal population are well established. Despite extensive efforts to integrate knowledge about sagittal parameters of the spine into surgical planning, there are still debates on which set of biomechanical parameters should be focused on to achieve the optimal surgical result for the individual patient. Unique IDentifier (UniD) Adaptive Spine Intelligence (ASI, Medtronic) makes spine surgery predictable and repeatable using artificial intelligence - backed by data science. Pre-operative planning with the integration of artificial intelligence mitigates the risk of surgical and realignment failure as well as revision surgery. Once the surgical plan has been decided on, the achievement of the surgical goal is directly related to surgical performance. Here, the placement of screws into the vertebral bodies is one of the main surgical steps in ASD surgery. Thanks to technical developments, the process of screw placement has advanced from conventional X-ray-guided and/or freehand techniques to navigated and robot-assisted techniques. In particular, the safety and reproducibility of screw placement have been claimed to be superior when using robotic assistance. In the present investigation, the primary objective is to evaluate the feasibility of software-based planning using the UniD ASI software in conjunction with robotic assistance and prebent rods during ASD surgeries with a focus on minimally invasive strategies for deformity correction. The secondary objective is to investigate both patient-reported outcome measures (PROMs) and patient-reported experience measures (PREMs). The hypothesis is that both software planning with the integration of artificial intelligence and robot-assisted minimally invasive surgeries provide a safe, reproducible, and significant improvement in clinical outcome in ASD patients.

title: NativeSeg: Native Vision Language Segmentation of 3D Computed Tomography via Spatial Visual Tokens and Verified Local Zoom
desc: Text prompted 3D computed tomography (CT) segmentation requires both full slice context and fine boundary precision across volumes where over $80\%$ of organ prompted slices lack the queried target. Existing medical vision language models (VLMs) are largely non native segmenters: they delegate pixel delineation outside the VLM by compressing reasoning into a 1D [SEG] vector for an external Segment Anything Model (SAM) decoder, quantizing masks into lossy discrete codebooks, or issuing box prompts to stateless external SAM tools without empty slice screening or spatial state memory. We introduce NativeSeg, a native vision language segmentation framework on Low Rank Adaptation (LoRA) adapted Qwen3.8-27B that performs dense mask decoding, volumetric triage, spatial error self diagnosis, and multiround local zoom directly over the VLM's 2D spatial visual tokens without external SAM decoders. NativeSeg decodes confidence maps from upper layer 2D spatial tokens fused with a five slice U-Net pathway, halts at zero zooms on $>91\%$ of standalone evaluations via a native presence gate ( ), localizes uncertain boundaries via a 20 cell multiscale error gate ( ), and accepts zoomed updates only when predicted error decreases. Trained solely on adult CT, NativeSeg improves Round $0$ DSC by $+19.81$ and $+7.04$ points over discrete codebook and 1D [SEG] readouts on the identical backbone, reaches $86.81\%$ adult and $87.04\%$ zero shot pediatric DSC, and safely refines 2D nnU-Net ($89.52\%$ adult; $86.86\%$ pediatric), 3D SegVol ($86.81\%$), and 3D VoxTell ($89.85\%$).

title: GENECraft: A Function- and Prior-Constrained Discrete Dynamical System for Controllable Regulatory DNA Design
desc: Designing regulatory DNA requires reconciling two complementary modeling paradigms: genomic language models (gLMs) capture evolutionary syntax without guaranteeing targeted regulatory activity, whereas sequence-to-function predictors provide explicit functional supervision without enforcing native-like sequence plausibility. We introduce GENECraft, a training-free Function- and Prior-Constrained Discrete Dynamical System (FP-DDS) that couples a genomic language model (Carbon) and a functional oracle (AlphaGenome) during inference-time optimization to balance predicted regulatory activity and consistency with genomic sequence priors. GENECraft evolves continuous latent nucleotide logits while evaluating strictly decoded discrete DNA sequences under a time-dependent composite vector field that fuses normalized functional utility, bidirectional contextual prior guidance, and compositional quality penalties, followed by feasibility-first trajectory readout. Across 2,185 loci spanning promoters, multi-constraint enhancers, and 18 transcription factors (TFs), GENECraft achieves full-joint success rates of 62.70%, 65.23%, and 94.56% (macro-averaged), substantially outperforming seven optimization, evolutionary, and generative baselines (which reach at most 2.15% on enhancers). In matched 336-locus ablations, in-loop Carbon guidance reduces native-relative dinucleotide divergence by 7.8--11.5%, enhancer context sensitivity by 10.5%, and TF mutation sensitivity by 11.0%, establishing FP-DDS as a principled framework for controllable regulatory DNA design.

title: Explainable and CPU-Efficient Brain Tumor Classification from MRI Using Two-Phase EfficientNetB3 Fine-Tuning
desc: Brain tumors are among the most lethal neurological disorders, with over 308,000 new diagnoses annually worldwide. Accurate classification of tumor type from Magnetic Resonance Imaging (MRI) scans is critical for treatment planning; however, manual radiological interpretation is time-consuming and prone to inter-observer variability. This paper proposes an automated deep learning pipeline for four-class brain MRI classification (glioma, meningioma, no tumor, and pituitary tumor) using EfficientNetB3 transfer learning with a custom classification head. A two-phase training strategy is adopted: Phase 1 trains the head with a frozen backbone (best validation accuracy: 92.77%), and Phase 2 selectively fine-tunes the top 37 layers at a 100x reduced learning rate (best validation accuracy: 94.91%). On an independent balanced test set of 1,600 MRI images, the system achieves 90.62% overall accuracy and a macro-average AUC of 0.9854. Gradient-weighted Class Activation Mapping (Grad-CAM) is integrated for class-discriminative visual explainability. The proposed system simultaneously addresses three dimensions absent in prior work: high accuracy, CPU-only computational efficiency, and clinical interpretability.

title: Flux Transformer learns intracellular metabolic fluxes from isotope labeling and measured reaction rates
desc: Cells convert incoming nutrients into energy and biomass via metabolic fluxes. Quantifying these fluxes involves feeding cells isotope-labeled nutrients, quantifying metabolite labeling patterns, and inverting the labeling data to retrieve the underlying flux distribution. Traditional metabolic flux analysis (MFA) is both computationally expensive and frequently requires manual refinement of the cost function to obtain plausible results. For this reason, MFA has remained inaccessible to non-experts. Here we present Flux Transformer, an AI model that uses reaction-specific attention to integrate isotope-labeling data with available reaction-rate measurements, reconstructing mass-balanced steady-state fluxes. The model is trained on simulated data with added noise and identifies the underlying fluxes from these data more effectively than traditional MFA. Provided experimental data from wild-type and mutant bacteria, yeast, plants, and mammalian T cells, it efficiently and accurately recovers expert-curated MFA fluxes. By making flux analysis accessible, Flux Transformer is poised to accelerate metabolic research and engineering.

title: Machine learning-guided discovery of TMX4@G electrocatalysts with LLM-assisted workflow automation.
desc: [Nanoscale] Coordination-engineered transition-metal single-atom catalysts offer a modular platform for the hydrogen evolution reaction (HER), but their discovery is hindered by the large configurational space arising from coupled metal-ligand variations. Here we develop a symmetry-aware and uncertainty-guided workflow to accelerate the screening of TMX4@G catalysts (X = C, N, O, P or S), where a transition-metal atom is coordinated by four ligands embedded in graphene. Canonicalization of rotationally equivalent motifs reduces 17 500 nominal structures to 4900 symmetry-inequivalent candidates while preserving chemical diversity. A cascaded Gaussian process regression model encodes a physical hierarchy from atomic descriptors to electronic structure, metal-hydrogen interaction and the HER activity. Posterior uncertainty drives active learning by balancing near-thermoneutral hydrogen binding with exploration of underrepresented coordination motifs. A large language model (LLM)-assisted automation framework further integrates structure generation, VASP input preparation, job submission, output parsing and dataset updating. DFT validation shows strong agreement with model predictions (R2 = 0.898 for 24 candidates) and identifies six thermodynamically stable catalysts with ηHER < 0.15 V.

title: AI-Guided Bronchoscopy Using the Broncho AI Navigator
desc: [Newly registered clinical trial, no results yet; sponsor: Ambu A/S; conditions: Bronchoscopy; type: INTERVENTIONAL; phase: NA; enrollment: 153; status: RECRUITING] This clinical investigation evaluates the Ambu Broncho AI Navigator, an investigational software system designed to provide real-time navigational support during bronchoscopy. The system uses artificial intelligence to identify and display airway anatomy during procedures and to help bronchoscopists track which airway segments have been examined. The study is conducted at Odense University Hospital and consists of two phases. In Phase 2a, experienced bronchoscopists use the system during routine bronchoscopies to evaluate and optimize technical settings and usability. For this phase 45 patients will be enrolled. In Phase 2b, bronchoscopies are randomized (1:1) to be performed with or without the Broncho AI Navigator to evaluate the impact of AI guidance on procedural performance. For this phase 108 patients will be enrolled. Adult patients undergoing elective bronchoscopy are enrolled, while the primary study subjects are the bronchoscopists performing the procedures. The study evaluates whether use of the Broncho AI Navigator improves bronchoscopy performance by increasing diagnostic completeness, improving structured progression through the bronchial tree, and reducing procedure time. The findings will support further development and future validation of the Broncho AI Navigator in clinical practice.

title: Rethinking Contrastive Targets in Radiology Language-Image Pretraining
desc: CLIP-style contrastive image-text pretraining is widely used in radiology data, where each image is paired with one report and every other report in the batch is treated as a negative. Under this recipe, two failures appear, neither of which is systematically addressed by existing contrastive learning theory: zero-shot evaluation peaks then degrades while training loss keeps decreasing, and training fails to learn from large batches. We hypothesize the cause is structural rather than radiology-specific: many unpaired reports share clinical findings with a given image, so CLIP's paired-identity target is systematically biased, not merely noisy. To test this, we construct CLEVR-Radiology, a synthetic testbed that preserves only this overlapping-fact structure and reproduces both failures. With evidence that the structure is sufficient to reproduce the failures, we develop a target-misspecification theory that explains both failures from a single deterministic gradient bias amplified by batch size, and use it to motivate a minimal compatibility-based correction, CorLIP: text is treated as positive whenever its clinical assertions agree with the image, with no architecture changes. Beyond benchmark improvements, CorLIP largely removes the post-peak degradation, makes large-batch training succeed where it previously collapsed, substantially amplifies the gains from more data, and is the only configuration that remains stable up to B=2048. The correction transfers from chest X-ray to 3D CT modalities.

title: ANCHOR: AI-NGS consensus hierarchy for optimized refinement of high-affinity binders from affinity maturation.
desc: [Briefings in bioinformatics] Affinity maturation for the systematic discovery of high-affinity protein reagents remains a major challenge in display-based protein engineering, largely because phenotypic enrichment frequently fails to correlate with true binding affinity. To improve candidate identification, we developed ANCHOR, an artificial intelligence (AI) and next-generation sequencing (NGS) consensus hierarchy for optimized refinement that implements a score-decoupled, two-stage strategy. Enrichment-trained classifier and regression models are used to construct a candidate pool, from which group-specific consensus sequences are subsequently derived without ranking candidates solely by individual model scores. Using the phosphotyrosine-binding Fyn SH2 domain as a model system, the two models achieved strong performance on untouched independent test sets (classification area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUROC) = 0.974; regression Pearson's r = 0.870). By leveraging a biopanning-guided filter, ANCHOR reduced the searchable sequence space by approximately four orders of magnitude while maintaining a ~90% overlap with exhaustive screening and retained 297 enrichment-predicted variants. These variants were grouped by residue identity at the least-conserved position (P4) and consensus sequences were derived within each group. Among the 16 evaluable consensus variants, 9 (56%) matched or exceeded the affinity of TrM, a previously established 100-fold-improved superbinder, with several showing a two-fold further improvement. Exploratory analyses using a structural proxy indicated robustness to parameter choices and a higher observed hit rate for ANCHOR than for the evaluated alternatives. Application to a public anti-HER2 scFv yeast-display NGS dataset demonstrated computational portability across datasets and library designs. Collectively, ANCHOR provides a practical framework for prioritizing affinity-maturation candidates from display-derived NGS data.

title: AI-Assisted Diabetes Education for Children With Type 1 Diabetes
desc: [Newly registered clinical trial, no results yet; sponsor: Yuzuncu Yil University; conditions: Type 1 Diabetes Mellitus; type: INTERVENTIONAL; phase: NA; enrollment: 60; status: RECRUITING] This randomized controlled study evaluates the effects of an artificial intelligence-assisted diabetes education video on quality of life, diabetes self-management skills, and glycemic control in children with type 1 diabetes mellitus. Participants are assigned to an intervention group receiving a 12-minute educational video through a Meta Quest 2 virtual reality headset or a control group receiving routine diabetes education and care. Outcomes are assessed at baseline and at three months using validated questionnaires and routinely recorded HbA1c values.

title: ProtoBridge-CLIP: Observation-Masked Finding Prototypes for Medical Image--Report Representation Learning
desc: Radiology reports distinguish affirmed findings, explicit negations, and unmentioned concepts, but conventional global image--report contrastive learning often compresses these different evidence states into a single study-level target. We introduce \model{}, which combines symmetric global image--report alignment with observation-masked finding supervision and a soft relation objective over affirmed report concepts. Text-derived finding prototypes are aligned with local visual tokens, while uncertain and unmentioned concepts are excluded from direct finding labels. We evaluate the framework on three CT benchmarks and five chest-radiograph benchmarks, together with component ablations, paired and clinical retrieval, localization, perturbation robustness, calibration, and per-finding analyses. \model{} achieves macro-AUROC values of 73.6%, 66.5\%, and 68.8% on CT-RATE, RAD-ChestCT, and INSPECT, and 80.2%, 91.4%, 78.5%, 86.5%, and 90.8% on ChestXray14, CheXpert, PadChest, RSNA, and SIIM-ACR, respectively. Relative to the matched global-only controls, the findings and relation objectives yield consistent gains across the evaluated datasets. These results demonstrate the practical value of treating observed and unobserved report concepts differently during medical image--text representation learning.
